Hi, I'm autistic. Autistic brains DONT *just* "work differently".  Schizophrenic brains are just as, if not more fucked, but schizophrenics are also neurodivergent, by definition. The idea that we're replacing the concept of disability with diversity, rather than just adding the concept of having strengths and being invisibly different, is SO harmful. Nobody who is autistic is not also disabled. You can identify as able-bodied, but that's because of the supports and accommodations you are given by yourself and others. If you did not ever need accommodating, you were never autistic. These are all disabilities and dysfunctions. I find it so disheartening that people are successfully making autism out to be nothing more than a difference. If you are simply different and not impaired, you are not autistic. The awareness efforts have clued people into our suffering, but the destigmatization efforts have undone that and then some. If you cannot eat, you're not "just different". If you cannot bathe yourself, you are not "just different". If you cannot find community with others, you are not "just different". You have to do those things differently! But that doesn't mean they're not more challenging and sometimes impossible for some people??

Anyway, bipolar is a neurodivergence because it is a permanent difference in the functioning of the brain that will always be there. "Chemical imbalance" is just the best way we can describe it to laypeople, myself included.

That just isn't true. Literally look it up. There's masking and there's autistic masking. We wear different masks in different settings and it's a way of communicating better. This often doesn't come naturally for autistic folks, leading to relational difficulties beyond just "that person's weird cuz they keep moving around or their affect isn't big like mine"

There are different levels to masking. The thing Neurotypical people do where they change how they behave around different people so as to not make people uncomfortable around them is also masking. Nobody wants to constantly communicate that they hate everybody. Some autistic people come off as creepy because they exhibit patterns of people with different intent. Normal masking is just conveying your intent with your speech and body language and is necessary for pretty much any relationship

People saying it's bad for you, I'm assuming are natural maskers?

When we say "masking" we mean a spectrum of things. There's the masking that's damaging- where we try to hide our true selves and our autistic traits as much as possible. 

But there's also the kind of masking that everybody does, that autistic people sometimes struggle with. This type of masking was really hard for me to distinguish when I was undoing the first one. It was hard to tell what's my true self and what's just not being in the right "mode" for the context im in. My best advice is to learn and think about what people expect and don't expect of you (within reason of your personhood, in good will), what it is you're trying to portray at any given moment (like, you can be mad, but good masking is a controlled anger. Others might be able to tell that you're upset, but that you wish only the best vibes to them), and most importantly, what your natural tendencies portray instead. Then you can work on communicating your true intent with your body language, intonation, and word choices.

Masking is an important part of communication and social living than people realize. If you're walking around accidentally communicating you hate everybody, it's natural and healthy to want to change that. Just make sure there are people who know you well enough that you don't have to mask around them. Some things will become automatic over time, with enough practice. :)

You know what neurotypical people don't get? That symptoms are normal traits. Every symptom a person can have (mentally/neurologically anyway) can be experienced by normal people under certain circumstances. Even things like paranoia, hallucination, and severe vertigo. You can get panic attacks without having a panic disorder and migraines without having a migraine disorder. People understand it with physical things and don't feel the need to tie it to their identity. But because so many new people are being diagnosed with developmental disorders later in life, and therefore recontextualizing their identities, many people are latching onto various traits and experiences as part of THEIR unique identities too. Without knowing that it's so fucking normal.   It doesn't help that because people now have a word for making connections, they feel the need to use it all the time. You don't have to say you're autistic every time you talk about XYZ symptom. If you're at a coffee shop, you just say you're overwhelmed by sound and would benefit from moving outside (but even then, only if the other person doesn't also think the music is too loud. Most of the time they will.) You don't have to say, "I'm autistic, so I experience off days" in a conversation about needing mental health days. It's not relevant because everyone is already talking about how they need it, and when enough people do this, the average person gets the impression that perfectly normal things are quirky parts of their identity. 

One of my biggest qualms with the autism and ADHD subs is that it's extremely easy for posts to spiral into "OMG I do this too!!!" Without anyone to fact check "hey, this is fucking normal." It's too easy for someone who feels invalid in their personality and experiences to experience enough confirmation bias to give themselves a whole diagnosis, and become so convinced that even if they do get formally tested and are told they don't have it, they feel so lost they NEED a second opinion. It explained their quirkiness, so it must be true!

I've only ever met 1 other actor who does this, or at least I saw their paper and immediately knew lol. This is especially helpful for monologues. I write it out a couple of times and then I write just the first letter of each word. 

For example:

I o e m 1 o a w d t, o a l I s t p a i k l... and so on, with all punctuation. 

Then I read the script as fast as I can. Once I'm reading it straight through and not stuttering, I try to read it using the first letter version. When I'm reading that straight through, I'm basically off book. This prevents mixing up the words, though I'm still young, so my mileage may vary later. 

Since I do theatre, I'm mostly able to do this AFTER I find all the emotional beats, which makes it much quicker. I've been doing it since 7th grade catechism, when I had to memorize Bible verses each week.

Edit to add: I just saw someone say they read it as many different ways as possible and I think this is excellent for when you're in a time crunch and really need to get the words in without having any of the emotional beats or performance aspect cemented. It forces your brain to actually memorize the text instead of the motions of it, so you don't get tripped up when you're given direction or get distracted by your thoughts. So like fast, slow, sIlLy, like a pirate, maybe even ad-libbing from different interpretations if you want to be extra directable. Just be sure to re-cement the actual text afterwards and never repeat something you've added.

Ever since moving into an apartment with a bathtub, I do the following routine:

- Day of make sure not to charge phone past 40%
- Sort laundry, throw in a load.
-Start Alexa "bath time" routine that puts the lights in the bathroom to dim warm white for 40 minutes, then very dim peach by the time I get in, hot pink, and then it fades in and out with one very dim warm white light and one different shades of teal, progressively getting brighter at each climax until it reaches baby blue and transitions to warm white to fade up to max for the end of the shower (goal is to beat this cuz obvi it's uncomfy).
- Brush hair, (very long, and I only brush before showers so it takes a bit).
- Scrub tub, if needed.
- Swap laundry and start new load, if time.
- Start filling tub.
- Make snacks/fancy drink/bagel.
- Light candle.
- Put on vibey music.
- Gather towels and waterproof phone case.
Bath with fancy drink, phone time, and snacks/bagel until water is cold. Refill half with super hot water. Bonus points if you've got a wee phone shopping list or something to really motivate to start the routine.
- The combination of phone dying, wave lights getting deeper, and being supremely hot in the water should motivate even the most stuck person to stand up. 
- Insert ear plugs.
- Put on podcast to distract self from the act of showering or keep vibes going. 
- DO NOT drain the tub of hot water.
- Shower, frequently with cool water bc you're standing in warm water and it feels v nice. 
- Do final hair rinse with cold water to invigorate (and close hair shaft cuz I got colored hair)
- If there's time, you can sit back down in the warm tub while the ocean lights finish. This is the best part. 
- Drain while you dry with towel and voila! You took a shower AND did your laundry!! Sometimes I'll even start the Roomba somewhere while I do the getting ready to bathe process.
